course_goals.text: Master the foundational principles and mechanics of deep learning, including core architectures, training dynamics, and optimization theory.
Analyze and apply advanced techniques for representation learning, data generation, and model adaptation across various domains.
Evaluate the theoretical limits and practical robustness of deep learning models, focusing on generalization, scaling, and inference.

L01.lecture_goal: Master the foundational principles and architectural components that drive modern deep learning.

objectives.text: You'll be able to understand the scope, requirements, and fundamental goals of the deep learning course.
You'll be able to trace the historical cycles of enthusiasm and decline in neural network development.
You'll be able to explain the fundamental mechanics of deep learning, including key components, the role of non-linearity, and how architecture enables generalization.
You'll be able to explain how deep networks are parameterized, trained using loss functions, and represent data through hierarchical building blocks.

L02.lecture_goal: master the theoretical foundations and practical mechanics of training neural networks, from optimization algorithms to backpropagation.

objectives.text: You'll be able to define the fundamental structure of neural networks and describe the core mechanisms of gradient-based optimization, including gradient descent, SGD, and momentum.
You'll be able to analyze the challenges posed by different loss landscapes and compare various optimization strategies to improve stability and convergence.
You'll be able to model neural networks using computation graphs and apply matrix calculus fundamentals to understand the forward pass.
You'll be able to explain how backpropagation calculates gradients and update parameters through linear and non-linear layers.
You'll be able to compare advanced neural system concepts and generalize the principles of backpropagation to arbitrary computational graphs.

L03.lecture_goal: analyze the theoretical foundations and practical limitations of using deep neural networks for function approximation.

objectives.text: You'll be able to frame the function approximation problem and establish the theoretical constraints for approximating Lipschitz functions.
You'll be able to derive and analyze the theoretical bounds for function approximation using ReLU networks.
You'll be able to compare different approximation methods and analyze the trade-offs between network width and depth.
You'll be able to critique the practical implications of theoretical results and discuss architectural scaling challenges in modern AI.

L04.lecture_goal: understand how architectural design choices, from basic perceptrons to advanced neural fields, dictate the capabilities and limitations of modern deep learning models.

objectives.text: You'll be able to analyze the fundamental differences between standard neural networks and specialized architectures like SIREN, focusing on how data and architectural inductive bias constrain the hypothesis space.

You'll be able to explain the mechanics and design principles of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), including how convolution filters detect patterns, achieve translation invariance, and manage dimensionality for a.

You'll be able to evaluate advanced CNN architectures by explaining the evolution of the receptive field, the function of encoder-decoder structures (like U-Net), and the role of skip connections in enhancing deep-net'.

You'll be able to apply modern deep learning techniques to complex data types by describing the use of 3D convolutions, positional encodings, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), and contemporary video processing models.

L05.lecture_goal: Analyze the theoretical foundations, architectural mechanics, and practical limitations of Graph Neural Networks.

objectives.text: You'll be able to understand the foundational concepts of graph modeling, including the role of GNNs in architectural constraints, classifying real-world graph problems, and defining necessary graph representation and,.
You'll be able to compare GNNs and CNNs, and explain the structural components and mechanics of message passing, relating these operations to standard neural network concepts.
You'll be able to explain the practical application and training procedure of GNNs using the message passing mechanism.
You'll be able to analyze the theoretical limitations of GNNs, discussing constraints based on graph equivalence classes and outlining practical requirements for their effective use.

L06.lecture_goal: compare classical and modern generalization theories to explain how deep neural networks achieve robust generalization despite high capacity.

objectives.text: You'll be able to outline the fundamental concepts of generalization theory, distinguishing between empirical and population risk, and analyzing how data and model structure influence generalization error.

You'll be able to design experiments to differentiate deep net generalization from memorization, illustrate out-of-distribution generalization, and explain how architectural biases contribute to generalization.
You'll be able to compare classical generalization theories (like VC theory) with modern phenomena such as double descent, and explain the role and limitations of Occam's razor in this context.
You'll be able to explain the specific mechanisms by which deep neural networks achieve generalization, including simplicity bias, low-rank solutions, and the impact of architectural symmetries.

L07.lecture_goal: master the theoretical and practical scaling rules necessary to stabilize and optimize deep learning models.

objectives.text: You'll be able to identify the fundamental challenges of optimization in deep learning and define the basic components of the optimization process.
You'll be able to compare first and second-order optimization methods, derive advanced techniques like Gauss-Newton, and understand their practical limitations.
You'll be able to analyze how different norms influence optimization stability, explain the necessity of non-Euclidean norms, and apply matrix norms to control network updates.
You'll be able to explain scaling rules for network width and depth and describe how optimization theory can be integrated into neural network architectures.

L08.lecture_goal: Understand the core principles, mechanisms, and diverse applications of the Transformer architecture.

objectives.text: You'll be able to identify the limitations of local processing methods and explain the necessity of global attention mechanisms in modern architectures.

You'll be able to define the fundamental data units of transformers, compare token-based processing to traditional neural network operations, and contrast the operational mechanisms of transformers with Graph Neural Nn.
You'll be able to derive and explain the mechanics of the attention mechanism, detailing how Query-Key-Value interactions and self-attention determine data relevance.

You'll be able to analyze the architectural efficiency of transformer layers, implement positional encodings, and apply the architecture to various tasks including vision and autoregressive language modeling.

L09.lecture_goal: Apply practical and theoretical knowledge to design, debug, and generalize robust deep learning models.

objectives.text: You'll be able to understand how to use practical heuristics and deep data inspection to analyze model results, identify spurious correlations, and validate input integrity.
You'll be able to compare and apply various data scaling and normalization techniques, and utilize tensor manipulation tools to prepare data for stable deep learning training.
You'll be able to explain how data augmentation, randomization, and high-dimensional inputs contribute to improved model generalization and predictive power.
You'll be able to apply best practices for selecting, training, and optimizing deep learning models, including interpreting loss metrics and utilizing advanced smoothing techniques.

L10.lecture_goal: compare and contrast various architectures used for sequence modeling, from basic RNNs to advanced memory and attention mechanisms, to understand the challenges of capturing long-term context in AI.

objectives.text: You'll be able to motivate the need for sequence modeling and understand the limitations of fixed-window convolutions.
You'll be able to define the structure and analyze the mechanisms and limitations of recurrent neural networks (RNNs).
You'll be able to explain advanced memory control mechanisms and compare different sequence generation architectures.
You'll be able to compare various sequence modeling architectures and evaluate the practical necessity and theoretical limits of long-term context.

L11.lecture_goal: master the principles, mechanisms, and applications of representation learning in deep neural networks.

objectives.text: You'll be able to understand the fundamental concepts of representation learning, including how neural networks encode data and how basic and deep layers perform geometric and non-linear transformations on input data.
You'll be able to explain the strategic importance of learned representations, covering their role in accelerating future learning through transfer learning and the necessity of massive pre-training.

You'll be able to evaluate the principles and methods of representation learning, defining the properties of good representations and comparing techniques like autoencoding, self-supervised learning, and masked data-to.

L12.lecture_goal: understand how contrastive learning and metric learning principles are applied to design and evaluate high-quality data representations.

objectives.text: You'll be able to explain the motivations for learning data representations and define the criteria for a good representation by comparing geometric properties of successful and failing representations.

You'll be able to compare linear and deep metric learning approaches by explaining how contrastive learning and metric learning mechanisms are formulated as constrained optimization problems using linear transformation.
You'll be able to analyze the specific mechanisms of contrastive loss by explaining how triplet loss and hard negative mining enforce similarity and accelerate learning in representation spaces.

You'll be able to describe the principles of self-supervised contrastive learning by explaining how data augmentations are used to create positive pairs and how repeated training leads to meaningful representations.

You'll be able to evaluate the effectiveness of contrastive learning by analyzing how alignment and uniformity metrics relate to loss behavior, and identifying critical components like augmentation and projection heads.

You'll be able to compare supervised and self-supervised learning objectives by analyzing how the similarity measure dictates effectiveness and how contrastive learning improves representation quality across different,.

L13.lecture_goal: explain the theoretical connections between neural networks, kernel methods, and Gaussian processes to understand the underlying principles of representation learning.

objectives.text: You'll be able to compare the efficiency of different training methods and understand how neural network architecture inherently expresses opinions about data similarity and function classes.
You'll be able to explain the mechanism of kernel methods, including Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces, and compare them to random function sampling methods.

You'll be able to understand the formal definitions of Gaussian processes, how they generalize Gaussian vectors, and how they perform inference and prediction using covariance functions and embeddings.

You'll be able to explain the theoretical correspondences between wide neural networks and Gaussian processes, and compare the practical reasons for preferring neural networks over kernel methods in deep learning.
You'll be able to evaluate the theoretical results of deep learning, including the role of weight initialization and the limitations of current design principles.

L14.lecture_goal: understand the foundational concepts, mathematical derivations, and diverse architectures of modern generative models.

objectives.text: You'll be able to outline the fundamentals of generative models, define them, and explain how conditioning creates a generative model.
You'll be able to illustrate the function of generative models and compare the direct and indirect approaches used to learn them.
You'll be able to derive the Max Likelihood objective and explain the mathematical mechanisms of energy-based models and Contrastive Divergence.
You'll be able to explain how autoregressive and diffusion models generate data and compare their mechanisms and efficiency.
You'll be able to explain the mechanism and adversarial process of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs).

L15.lecture_goal: understand the theoretical foundations and practical mechanisms of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) as a bridge between representation learning and generative modeling.

objectives.text: You'll be able to compare representation learning and generative modeling as inverse processes, and identify the limitations of using autoencoder decoders for generative sampling.
You'll be able to define latent variable models, explain the mathematical structure of Mixture of Gaussians (MoG), and describe the framework for sampling from these models.

You'll be able to explain the computational challenges of likelihood maximization and apply Monte Carlo methods, including the reparameterization trick and importance sampling, to approximate marginal likelihoods.
You'll be able to derive and explain the components of the Variational Autoencoder (VAE) objective function, including the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO).
You'll be able to analyze how the tension between compression and reconstruction shapes the VAE latent space, and explain how VAEs learn structured and disentangled representations.

L16.lecture_goal: master the principles and advanced architectures of conditional generative models for complex, multimodal data generation.

objectives.text: You'll be able to define the challenges of structured prediction and compare classical methods to generative models for handling complex, multimodal data.
You'll be able to explain the mechanisms of core conditional generative models, including Conditional GANs, Conditional VAEs, and autoregressive models.
You'll be able to analyze how modern transformer-based architectures integrate and condition generative models on diverse data types, such as text and images.

L17.lecture_goal: understand the fundamental challenges of model generalization and evaluate advanced techniques for building robust machine learning systems.

objectives.text: You'll be able to analyze how distribution shifts and adversarial examples expose the brittleness and weaknesses of deployed machine learning models.
You'll be able to explain how data biases and realistic distribution shifts impact generalization, and describe how Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) addresses these issues.
You'll be able to evaluate various practical strategies and trade-offs for improving model robustness and generalization against distribution shifts.

L18.lecture_goal: Master the principles, techniques, and modern applications of transfer learning, from foundational concepts to large foundation models.

objectives.text: You'll be able to outline the scope of the transfer learning mini-series and apply few-shot learning concepts to understand pattern recognition challenges.
You'll be able to explain the core motivation and mechanism of transfer learning, and analyze the different types of knowledge transfer and implementation bottlenecks.
You'll be able to explain the mechanisms of fine-tuning and self-supervised pretraining, and adapt pre-trained models when input or output dimensions change.
You'll be able to describe methods for fine-tuning models and mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and analyze the mechanisms and motivations behind domain adaptation.
You'll be able to explain knowledge distillation by matching teacher and student prediction distributions, and compare distillation and compression techniques for creating efficient, smaller models.

You'll be able to explain the definition and utility of foundation models in transfer learning, analyze the environmental and societal costs associated with training large foundation models, and compare various methods.

L19.lecture_goal: understand the theoretical foundations, practical applications, and advanced trade-offs associated with using generative models for data augmentation and representation learning.

objectives.text: You'll be able to explain how generative models function to access and manipulate data beyond the original training set using latent variables.
You'll be able to analyze how latent space exploration and interpolation techniques improve data representation and disentanglement.
You'll be able to apply generative models to practical tasks such as labeling synthetic data, probing biases, and evaluating medical data.
You'll be able to evaluate the theoretical contributions of generative models to knowledge representation and address associated challenges.
You'll be able to compare the application of generative methods with advanced meta-learning approaches.

L20.lecture_goal: master the principles of scaling laws to strategically design, optimize, and predict the performance of large deep learning models.

objectives.text: You'll be able to define scaling laws and understand their foundational importance in deep learning, referencing key concepts like 'The Bitter Lesson'.
You'll be able to explain the strategic framework for efficiently designing and training large models using scaling laws, differentiating between loss and performance scaling.
You'll be able to analyze the core optimization problem and define the mathematical relationships (power laws) governing model loss and performance based on resources.
You'll be able to model the optimal resource allocation by describing the Pareto front and explaining how model size and data size interact to maximize performance.
You'll be able to apply the derived scaling laws to optimize model training resources and evaluate their predictive power across various domains.

L21.lecture_goal: understand the progression of language models, from foundational architectures to advanced alignment techniques that enable complex reasoning.

objectives.text: You'll be able to explain the historical evolution of language models, from early count-based approaches to modern architectures and the shift toward transfer learning.
You'll be able to analyze the mechanisms of in-context learning, comparing the limitations of masked language modeling with the capabilities and debates surrounding prompt-based model steering.
You'll be able to describe how scaling and advanced prompting techniques, such as Chain-of-Thought, enable large language models to acquire and demonstrate complex reasoning capabilities.

You'll be able to compare various methods for controlling and aligning large language models, including instruction tuning, addressing failure modes, and implementing Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).

L23.lecture_goal: understand the theoretical foundations and advanced optimization techniques required for stable and efficient deep learning.

objectives.text: You'll be able to define the theoretical framework for building and optimizing deep learning models.
You'll be able to analyze the structural properties and constraints of well-normed modules.
You'll be able to explain advanced optimization techniques using dual-to-primal conversion.

L24.lecture_goal: understand the spectrum of inference, search, and adaptation methods used to drive intelligent and self-improving deep learning systems.

objectives.text: You'll be able to differentiate between core deep learning processes and foundational search strategies by explaining the roles of training, inference, and test-time compute.

You'll be able to compare and contrast various generative sampling and search methods by analyzing autoregressive inference, greedy sampling limitations, and techniques for obtaining high-likelihood samples.
You'll be able to analyze advanced optimization and search paradigms by describing how scoring functions, multi-objective optimization, and human feedback drive generative model improvement.
You'll be able to evaluate modern adaptation techniques by comparing in-context learning to gradient descent and explaining how self-supervised test-time training enables self-improvement.
